Before any AI reads your resume, a filter may have already removed you.

Pin, an AI recruiting platform, audited more than 33,000 jobs and 37,000 recruiter searches run through its system, and found that 70.7 percent of those searches apply an employer prestige filter. In plain terms, a prior brand name employer is required before a human or a machine looks at anything else.

And 96 percent of minimum tenure filters sit at exactly 12 months. That is not a recruiter making a judgment call. That is a platform default.

So if your last role lasted nine months because of a layoff, a contract ending, or a restructuring, you can be filtered out before anyone reads what you actually did there. If your employers are solid companies without famous names, same result. The filter does not ask why. It just removes you.

This is the part of the hiring story nobody tells you, because it happens before the story starts.

Do not fix it by inventing a longer tenure or a bigger employer on the page. That is exactly how people end up in the situation from my last post, sitting across from someone who runs that function, unable to walk through a number that never happened.

What you can control is what a reader sees first when you do get through. Lead with the scope of the work and the result it produced, not with a date range that invites a filter to do the thinking. Make the first lines answer the only question that matters: what did this person actually change.

🚨 Two users update the same record in your .NET application.

Both requests succeed.

But one user's changes disappear.

No exception. No obvious failure.

This is the classic lost update problem, and it's a good reminder that database correctness requires more than successful API responses.

Imagine an enterprise ASP.NET Core application:

1️⃣ User A reads a record.
2️⃣ User B reads the same record.
3️⃣ User A updates and saves it.
4️⃣ User B submits an update based on older data.

Without appropriate concurrency handling, User B's update may overwrite User A's changes.

The challenge becomes more important in applications handling approvals, inventory, claims, financial transactions, and shared business records.

Some practical strategies include:

✅ EF Core optimistic concurrency tokens
✅ SQL Server rowversion columns
✅ Detecting DbUpdateConcurrencyException
✅ Returning HTTP 409 Conflict where appropriate
✅ Reloading and comparing conflicting changes
✅ Pessimistic locking for selected workflows
✅ Transaction isolation based on business requirements
✅ Idempotency for retryable operations
✅ Integration tests covering concurrent updates

The important distinction:

A transaction can be atomic without preventing every business-level concurrency conflict.

And the right solution depends on whether the application should reject, merge, retry, or serialize competing updates.

💬 QUESTION FOR THE .NET COMMUNITY

How do you typically handle concurrent updates in enterprise applications?
A) EF Core optimistic concurrency
B) Database locking
C) Application-level version checks
D) Workflow-specific conflict resolution

What has worked best in your systems? 👇

Your AI research tool gets roughly 1 in 6 answers wrong.

• That’s not a guess. Stanford researchers tested the legal-specific AI tools, including Lexis+ AI and Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, and found they hallucinated between 17% and 33% of the time.
• The obvious errors aren’t the real danger. The quiet ones are.

Stanford calls them “misgrounded” answers: a real case, a real citation, cited for a point it doesn’t actually support. It looks perfect in the draft. It only falls apart when someone pulls the case and reads it.

And courts are noticing:
⚖️ Mata v. Avianca: $5,000 in sanctions for a brief citing six cases that didn’t exist
⚖️ 1,240 reported instances of AI-generated fake content in U.S. court filings since April 2023 (Maryland State Bar Association)
⚖️ ABA Formal Opinion 512: lawyers should never rely on or submit AI output without appropriate independent verification.
⚖️The answer isn’t to stop using AI. It’s to stop letting the verification step land on the attorney at 9 p.m. the night before a filing.

Here’s what well-run firms do:
•Define every research assignment in writing: jurisdiction, question, sources, format, deadline.
•Keep supported facts separate from assumptions.
•Check every citation against the actual authority, including pincites and quotes.
•Keep a citation review log of what was checked and what’s still open.
•Treat AI as a first draft, never a final answer.

That’s the workflow behind Remote Legal Team’s attorney-directed research support:
1.Research instructions
2.AI outline draft
3.Human source check
4.Attorney approval

Our remote paralegals handle authority research, case summaries, draft memoranda, motion support, and citation checking. You receive a research memorandum, an authority matrix, case law summaries, a citation review log, and draft work product labeled for your review.

Strategy, advice, and final approval stay with your attorneys. Always.
AI drafts. A trained person checks. Your attorney approves.

Number 10 is hiring someone to advise the Prime Minister on how AI will change jobs.

Dear Downing Street, I’d like to apply. 👋

Last week at UNLEASH Paris I moderated two sessions on the AI-amplified organisation, with some of the biggest HR tech and consulting names in the room. The conversation has moved on. Nobody is asking whether AI will reshape work any more. They’re asking who ends up owning what it creates.

That’s the question this role has to answer. And the window to answer it is closing fast.

Within the next 6 to 12 months, digital twins will hit the market at scale. Agents trained on how a specific person thinks, decides and solves problems. Built from their judgement, their experience, their intelligence architecture.

Right now, by default, the employer keeps all of it. The person walks away with nothing when the contract ends. Our employment law was written for people who sell their time. It has nothing to say about a digital version of you that keeps working after you’ve gone.

If we don’t legislate before these products land, we won’t be regulating a market. We’ll be retrofitting one. And we know how that goes.

From a FusionWork perspective, the job comes down to three things.

1. Ownership. A digital twin is built from a person’s intelligence, so the person owns it. Full stop. Put that in law before the first contract templates set the norm.

2. Value creation. Back AI in the loop with humans, not humans in the loop with AI. One route amplifies people and creates new value. The other strips cost, puts a human on sign-off duty and calls it augmentation. Only one of them grows the tax base.

3. Wealth that flows back to its source. Treat the twin as an asset. The person licenses it to their employer while they work there and takes it with them when they leave, like a pension. When it creates value for the business, a share flows directly back to the human who built the intelligence behind it.

Not redistribution after the fact. Distribution designed in from the start.

And it fixes a problem the Treasury hasn’t clocked yet. Digital workers pay no income tax, no NI, and buy nothing on the high street. That’s Ghost GDP: growth on paper, missing from the public finances. Licence income is taxable income. Taxable income gets spent. Ghost GDP becomes real GDP, in real postcodes.

As for this week’s jobs pledges, 22,400 apprenticeships a year and 200,000 entry-level tech roles are welcome. But entry level is exactly the rung organisations are removing first. Adding places while firms saw off the bottom rung isn’t a skills strategy. It’s how Labour Debt gets built.

So, Kanishka Narayan MP, Lord Vallance, whoever is drafting that job spec: the person in this seat shouldn’t be explaining disruption to workers. They should be making sure workers own what their intelligence creates.

I’ve got the research, the framework and the draft legislative architecture. Happy to bring the kettle. ☕

If your AI made 1 wrong decision today, which would cost you most?

MIT mapped the answer from 30 interviews with 27 executives

Their study covered 9 global companies.

They found that every decision can be sorted by 2 things:

→ Ambiguity: is there one clear answer?
→ Risk: what does a wrong call cost?

The second question is the one you just answered

That gives you 4 lanes, with a different AI role in each:

⚙️ 𝟭. 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗲

Clear answer, cheap mistake.

→ AI runs it, you spot check the patterns
→ Lead follow ups, booking reminders...
→ At telecom One New Zealand, an agent cut audience building time by 60%
→ The team still reviews the plan before launch

🛡️ 𝟮. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹

Clear answer, costly mistake.

→ AI does the work, you own the exceptions
→ Refunds, invoices, price replies
→ Set the limits before it starts
→ One NZ's agents resolve 60%+ of app questions under one rule: a price is never wrong

🧪 𝟯. 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆

Fuzzy answer, cheap mistake.

→ You + AI shape the idea together
→ New offers, ad angles, subject lines
→ A wrong guess costs little, so test more ideas before you spend money

🎯 𝟰. 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰

Fuzzy answer, costly mistake.

→ AI pulls the research, you make the call
→ Hiring, pricing, which service to drop
→ One NZ runs 15 agents on its network data, and humans make the tradeoff calls

My take on using this:

The decision you thought of at the top most likely sits in lane 2 or lane 4.
So keep a person on it.

For your business start with lane 1.
That's where AI pays back first and a mistake costs the least.

The lane can change later.

Drafting a refund reply is routine.
Approving the refund is consequential.

So move a decision to a tighter lane if:
Money, a client or a contract is attached to it.

And give every AI a named owner.

So which decision in your business is routine today but still done by hand?

Depleting liquid runway while attempting to maintain household cash requirements.

I faced this reality firsthand. After 25 years directing distribution expansion across 30+ European markets, private-equity consolidation dismantled our field compensation by up to 90% in months.

Remaining passive wasn't an option. But jumping back into another extractive corporate hierarchy would have been repeating the exact same risk failure.

Autonomous Operational Leverage: Modern infrastructure eliminates administrative drag. Automated qualifying funnels paired with 24/7 AI conversational closers handle prospect inquiries and conversions without expanding payroll or demanding 60-hour workweeks.
A corporate layoff is a disruption, not a destination. Reinvest your talent into an asset where you retain the equity and control the outcome.

Last month I wrote about why cutting cyber budgets is usually the wrong place to save. Since then, many of my conversations have come back to a different problem, which is finding the right people in the first place.
Across Germany and the rest of Europe, many organisations are still struggling to fill their cyber roles, especially at senior level. NIS2 holds management accountable for cyber risk, but it doesn’t require a full-time CISO, which for most SMEs wouldn’t be realistic anyway. What I see quite often is that important security decisions are put on hold until the right person is hired, while the risk stays exactly where it was.
There are effective ways to close that gap without waiting for the hiring market. A vCISO can take care of strategy, governance and board reporting in a few days a month. Contract specialists and Talent as a Service bring in hard-to-hire skills such as OT security, cloud and identity, or audit readiness when a project or deadline calls for them. AI-assisted compliance and AI governance help scarce experts spend their time on decisions rather than on paperwork.
Whichever route you take, write down why you chose it. A risk-based plan that explains how you covered the gap is much easier to defend than a role that has been vacant for months.

Ever wondered why you can sit through six hours of Netflix on high alert but start to day dream on a demo? 

Because a gazillion things happen to your grey jelly when you hear a story. Luckily, I’ll only cover 5 below: 

🧠 Our brains ignore whatever stays the same - think laundry list of features. The moment something changes, the brain ‘lights up’. Every good story opens with a hook - something has changed. Attention grabbed. 

🧠 When you’re curious about ‘who killed that guy’? your brain’s reward system is turned on. In B2B, say “Two of your competitors halved their onboarding time this year. Only one of them did it without hiring.” Now your buyer wants to know which one, and how. Everything you say before you reveal that gets remembered too.

🧠 The buyer plays the scene out in their head. When a relatable character does something, the same parts of our brain fire as if we were doing it ourselves. This means that when  you tell a CFO about a peer who missed a quarter, they live through a small version of that quarter themselves.

🧠 Buyers disagree way less. When you read a sales contract you check for every way you can be screwed. But, once you’re absorbed in a story, all that energy goes into following the plot instead. 

🧠 The listener’s brain syncs up with the storyteller’s. The closer the sync, the better they understand. No sync - no understanding. That’s what category jargon does to your buyer. Say “AI-native unified data orchestration layer,” and their brain stops syncing with yours.

This post is for the folks in “build it and they will come” camp. 

Science says otherwise. They won’t if there is no narrative. 

Build one. Rooted in science.

*Is the #Job_hiring less or stalled in the #Indian_private_sector job market?*
In the Indian private sector, especially in #IT services and #software_product  based companies, a vacancy being advertised does not necessarily mean the employer is ready to hire immediately. Some roles are delayed, put on hold, dependent on client approval, or cancelled after interviews.

**What current employment data says — India, October 2026**

Why are candidates finding it difficult to secure jobs?
1. Salary and budget constraints
The hiring manager may want a candidate but have a fixed salary budget. Experienced candidates may be rejected because their expectations exceed that budget, while candidates willing to accept less may be prioritised.

2. Client-dependent projects
In service-based companies, hiring can depend on a confirmed project, client approval, funding, or a signed contract. A position may be discussed with candidates before all these conditions are finalised.

3. More competition for suitable roles
Layoffs, project closures, contract expirations and voluntary job changes all add candidates to the market. Even when hiring continues, a particular vacancy can attract many applicants with similar experience.

4. Delayed or uncertain recruitment
Interviews may be completed while HR waits for budget approval, feedback from the hiring manager, client confirmation or a final decision. Some vacancies are frozen or cancelled without timely communication to candidates.

5. Changing skill requirements
Employers increasingly prioritise candidates who can demonstrate specialised skills and broader business impact. AI is also changing some roles, reducing demand for certain tasks while creating demand for other capabilities.

**Conclusion**
The present situation is not simply that companies have stopped hiring. It is that hiring demand, available budgets, skill requirements and actual job offers are not moving at the same pace.

The right question is not only “Are companies hiring?” but also “How many advertised positions are approved, funded, suitable for my experience, and likely to result in an actual offer?”

Is the biggest risk in adopting AI recruitment technology no longer the technology itself, but who carries the liability when something goes wrong?

I've noticed a significant shift in enterprise attitudes towards AI adoption. Compliance, accountability and legal exposure are moving much higher up the procurement agenda.

And with good reason.

The ongoing Workday litigation, alongside investigations involving providers including Greenhouse, should make every HR technology buyer ask some uncomfortable questions.

In the Workday case, allegations of discriminatory applicant screening have been allowed to proceed, although liability hasn't been established. Workday maintains that customers control their own hiring decisions.

But consider the implications.

When technology providers emphasise that clients control the decisions, configurations and outcomes, where does that leave employers who trusted the technology?

Some might call it throwing clients under the bus. It certainly exposes a potential divide between what vendors sell and what customers believe they're buying.

Procurement teams need to examine contractual clauses transferring compliance obligations to customers, alongside configuration tools allowing employers to set scoring thresholds, rankings and automated rejection rules.

Being able to configure something doesn't make it compliant. Nor does a contractual disclaimer automatically remove a vendor's legal responsibilities.

The EU AI Act's high-risk recruitment requirements, currently scheduled for December 2027, raise the stakes further. Screening, ranking and selection systems face obligations covering risk management, data governance, transparency, record-keeping and human oversight.

Automated rejection, discriminatory scoring, opaque assessments and decisions nobody can explain or challenge deserve particular scrutiny.

Before signing another AI technology contract, I'd be asking:

 Who is legally responsible for AI decisions?

 Can we validate the assessments and scoring?

 Can we explain, audit and challenge decisions?

 What compliance evidence will the vendor provide?

 What happens when the technology causes harm?

This isn't just an enterprise problem. SMEs face many of the same risks, often without the legal resources to defend themselves.

For AI innovators, the message is equally important. Compliance cannot simply become the customer's problem after implementation.

The next competitive advantage in recruitment technology may not be what AI can automate, but what its developers can prove is safe, fair and accountable.

In one of my early in-house recruitment gigs I had a technical role reporting into one of the Directors. This was a mid size manufacturing business.

We were reviewing candidates and he was keen to bring one in for interview.

I said I didn't think she was right, to which he replied, "she has six sigma so she can do the job".

I disagreed too mildly, probably muttering under my breath about context fit or something.

You see she worked for a large, as in very large, systemised pharmaceutical manufacturer. Her CV showed she worked in a large team. It seemed like a job of structure, change requests and bureaucracy. Rather than a standalone, deal with the chaos, make a name for yourself and help leadership understand what's going wrong, type vacancy we had.

This might seem the same assumption he made, but there's a key difference. His knowledge was based on few employers, the ones he worked in, and the ones he recruited from.

Mine was based on having recruited across the region for 12 years, at that point. I'd already come across people from that company, at different levels. I just didn't articulate that insight well enough.

It's the kind of contextual insight you can now start to investigate with LLM queries.

Anyway he interviewed the candidate who travelled 90 minutes. Both agreed the interview wasn't right.

Chap who got the job had been a consultant. On paper might not have seen a fit, but he showed how he had been in the weeds of many smaller businesses, and given he always had to justify his costs to win and repeat contracts, his influencing was a boon.

I don't think the hiring manager liked me much - he kept throwing acronyms at me, and making passive aggressive comments in the HR team. I quite liked him.

I'm sure there were loads of lessons to take from this little microcosm of recruitment, such as what happens behind the page is more important than what's on the page.

Mind you if you only ever rely on the page, like a lot of AI recruitment, that might be a problem.

Two weeks, one real feature, and no need for another round of interviews.

That is how a founder described an engineering hire in a recent podcast clip. The candidate got a specific feature to build, asked questions, found their way around the codebase, and shipped it. After that, there was no longer any doubt about whether this person could do the job.

We think the same logic applies when a company chooses an engineering or AI partner.

Long evaluations tend to measure presentation: decks, case studies, references, rate cards. They rarely show how a team actually works on your code, with your constraints and your people.

A small, paid, fixed-scope trial tells you more:

How fast does the team understand an unfamiliar system?
What questions do they ask in the first days?
How visible is the work while it happens: commits, reviews, progress updates?
What is actually delivered at the end, and could your own team maintain it?

It costs a few weeks. It can save months with the wrong partner.

For AI work, the equivalent is a short pilot on your own data, with one clear success measure agreed upfront.

How do you test a partner today before signing a long contract?

The job hunt has changed. Are we changing with it?

Job searching in 2026 can feel strangely contradictory.

Unemployment may look stable, yet many candidates are spending months searching. Employers are not hiring at pace, but many still say they cannot find the right skills. Meanwhile, AI has made it easier than ever to apply and much harder to stand out.

Here is what I am seeing:
•	Applications per role have surged; LinkedIn reports candidates are submitting about 30% more applications than before the pandemic.

•	The average time to fill a role has risen from 41.4 days in 2022 to 61.5 days in the first eight months of 2026.

•	More than 27% of job seekers have been searching for 27 weeks or longer.

•	Employers increasingly use AI screening, while candidates use AI to tailor applications creating an “AI versus AI” bottleneck.

•	Skills-based hiring is growing, with many employers prioritising demonstrated capability over traditional qualifications.

So the question is no longer simply: “How many jobs can I apply to?”

It is: “How do I become memorable, credible, and discoverable in a crowded market?”

Some new rules I believe are worth discussing:

1.	Stop spraying, start positioning. A smaller number of well researched, well targeted applications will usually beat a high volume approach.

2.	Use AI as a thinking partner, not a replacement. Let it help you structure ideas but bring your own evidence, outcomes, voice, and judgement.

3.	Make your skills visible. Portfolios, case studies, projects, certifications, talks, writing, and measurable results matter more than a polished but generic CV.

4.	Prioritise humans, not just portals. Referrals, genuine networking, alumni connections, and conversations with people inside target companies can cut through automated screening.

5.	Treat the search like a campaign. Track outreach, follow up thoughtfully, build relationships, and review what is working every week.

6.	Stay open to non linear routes. Contract work, project-based roles, internal moves, and adjacent industries can create momentum when permanent roles are scarce.

The market is difficult but it is not closed. Healthcare, skilled trades, and other demand driven sectors continue to hire, while employers remain selective about capability and fit.

Over to you: What has changed most in your own job search over the past year? And what is one tactic that has actually helped you get noticed?
